Strong margins against sampled training negatives do not establish full-catalog ranking quality. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; popularity sampling is therefore no automatic correction for uniform sampling. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/). A 2024 sequential-recommendation study found that aggregate performance concealed substantial head/mid/tail differences, with random-negative training favoring head items. This supports checking low-frequency Electronics targets separately, but does not establish their behavior in this dataset. [Prakash et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276). RecSys 2025 research likewise examines sampling reliability through fidelity, resolution, robustness and recovery of preference-based model rankings. [On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086).

Suggested diagnostic, inferred from these findings: freeze one GRU4Rec checkpoint per category and compare identical users/targets under fixed uniform negatives, training-frequency-weighted negatives, negatives matched to the target’s training-frequency band, and title-similar distractors built from available text without pretrained weights. Keep candidate counts equal, sample unique distractors, exclude observed history, and document each sampler. Add chunked full-catalog scoring with the same checkpoint, preserving exact ranks and history exclusions. Report HR@10 changes, target-rank shifts, failure-set overlap and results by training-frequency band. Title similarity is a proposed stress test, not a proven relevance label; unobserved distractors can be relevant. Retain the pinned host macro validation HR@10 as the selection criterion. Label training-prefix measurements as fit diagnostics, and full-catalog measurements as catalog-ranking diagnostics—not unbiased preference estimates or held-out performance when computed on training prefixes.
